headline: Captree dock talk: ocean's a washing machine, so we're fishing the inlet seam
subhead: With 3-4 foot swell rolling outside, the fluke, bass, and blues have crowded into Fire Island Inlet and the bay's deep channels — and that's exactly where I've been.
body_markdown:
Had a guy at the dock this morning, tackle still shrink-wrapped, asking if he should run his 21-footer out past the inlet for some deep-water action. I looked at him, looked at the swell breaking white over the outer bar, and said, "Buddy, you'll spend more time bailing than fishing." That's been the story all week — 3 to 4 feet of leftover ocean swell stacked up on a short period, the kind that turns a nice morning into a chore if you're not set up for it. So I told him what I've been telling everybody who'll listen: leave the open water alone this week and fish the seams. The inlet and the bay are holding fish, and honestly, they're holding better fish than the beach front is right now.

Here's the why. Offshore, the Bight is sitting around 76 degrees on the surface with that swell rolling through — not dangerous, but sloppy enough that bait and predators alike are ducking for cover. That pushes everything toward structure, and there's no better structure on this whole stretch of coast than Fire Island Inlet and the channels running off it. Fluke have piled onto the deeper water around the Robert Moses bridges — I'm talking 30 to 45 feet, right along the pilings and the current break where the sand drops off into the channel. Outgoing tide has been the move, dragging white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails nice and slow along bottom, letting the current do the work instead of ripping it. Picked up a mixed bag Tuesday morning — a few shorts, one heavy 5-pounder that came off the west side of the second bridge on a chartreuse bucktail tipped with squid strip. Nothing to write home about in numbers, but the quality's there if you're patient and you're willing to drift it three or four times before committing to a spot.

Striped bass are doing what they do in August — going nocturnal and staying close to bait. Bunker schools are still working the beach and pushing into the inlet on the tide changes, and the bass are shadowing them, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing when everything funnels out of the bay through Fire Island Inlet. Live-lined bunker on a fish-finder rig, fished tight to the rip line off Democrat Point at first light or after dark, has been the ticket. I had two solid fish — one just over 30 inches — off the point Wednesday at sunrise, both on bunker chunks fished on the bottom in maybe 15 feet of water where the rip pushes out past the jetty rocks.

Worth mentioning for anybody who hasn't heard: Heckscher State Park opened up night fishing on a trial basis this summer, Field 6 only, Friday through Sunday, dusk to dawn, through Labor Day. You need the Night Sport Fishing Permit or the 4x4 permit on your dash, but if you've got it, that stretch of Great South Bay shoreline is worth a look on an outgoing tide — the bay's dumping warm water and bait right past there, and it's the kind of quiet structure edge that summer bass like to work after dark. I haven't fished it myself yet this trial run, but I've got it circled for next week if the wind cooperates.

Bluefish have been the most reliable fun on calm mornings — and we've had a few of those between swell events. Bunker pods are getting worked over right off the beach from Kismet down past Cherry Grove, and when the blues get under them it's blitz fishing, plain and simple. Poppers, metal, doesn't matter much — get near the commotion and cast into it. Just watch your leader, these aren't snapper-sized, some of these cocktail blues are pushing 3 to 4 pounds and they'll chew through light mono without blinking.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, have been thin. A few reports of fish coming out of the deeper holes off Patchogue and around the West Sayville flats on bucktails at dusk, but it's not a pattern yet, more like scattered luck. What I am watching closely is peanut bunker — we flagged a couple weeks back that they'd be pushing into Great South Bay behind the New England run, and I'm starting to see small pods of them stacking in the back creeks off Bellport and Patchogue on the last of the ebb. If that holds, the weakfish and the cocktail blues both should tighten up behind them over the next week or two — peanuts draw everything in this bay once they show.

Looking ahead, if this swell backs off like the pattern suggests, I'd keep an eye on the outer sandbars off Robert Moses and Democrat Point late in the week. Surface temps pushing past 70 out there means it's not crazy to think the first false albacore or bonito of the season could show up chasing bait balls along the beach — it's happened before around this calendar mark. I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet, but I'll have a small metal rod rigged and ready just in case, because that's the kind of surprise you don't want to miss because you left the right lure at home.
